title: Late-Binding Lambdas
code:
fns = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])

fns = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fns])
explanation:
A closure captures the **variable**, not its value at the time. All three lambdas refer to the same `i`, which is only looked up when the lambda is *called*. By then the loop has finished and `i` is `2`.

In the second version, `i=i` is a default argument, and defaults are evaluated when the lambda is *created*, so each lambda stores the current value.

(Yes, this is the same "defaults are evaluated once at definition time" rule that causes the mutable-default-argument bug, used on purpose here.) `functools.partial` is another clean fix.

sources.title: Python FAQ: Why do lambdas defined in a loop all return the same result?
